title: Arjuna picks up his bow
hookLine: more than six hundred verses after he dropped it, Arjuna is ready to pick up his bow
tomorrow: a ghost that must be kept busy, and a dog's tail that won't stay straight
last: YOUR OWN DUTY, DONE WITH CARE.

lines: THE BOW ON THE CHARIOT FLOOR.
cards: Remember Arjuna's bow, lying on the floor of the chariot? It's still there. The armies still face each other.
More than six hundred verses have passed since it slipped from his hand: almost the whole Gita, everything Krishna has taught him. And now, near the very end, Krishna asks two questions.
Did you hear this with a focused mind? Is your confusion gone? Arjuna answers: my confusion is gone.
My memory has come back. My doubts are gone, and I'll do as you say. The Gita doesn't stop to show his hands, but the war that follows makes it plain: he picks up the bow.

teach.b: What changed his mind? Not a new job. Same battlefield, same duty.
What changed is how he holds it. A little earlier in chapter eighteen of the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna gives the line karma yoga leans on more than almost any other.
Paraphrased: the one from whom all beings come, by whom all this is spread out, worshiping that one with your own work, a person reaches perfection. Svakarmana tam abhyarcya.
With your own work, worship. Not someone else's work. Not a holy job you'll get around to someday.
Your own. You can see it in a lot of Hindu kitchens.

teach.h: THE FIRST ROTI FOR THE SHRINE.
teach.b: The first roti off the pan, or the first spoon of rice, goes on a little plate before the family's shrine, or to the cow outside, or to the birds. Nobody thinks the gods are starving.
The cooking itself has been offered, and what was set before the shrine is taken back as prasad, a blessing. Then everyone eats.
Vivekananda carried this into the street: serve people as you'd serve God, because God is in them. That became the heart of the Ramakrishna Mission, which he founded in 1897.
And chapter two says what offered work looks like from outside: yoga is skill in action. Offered work isn't sloppy work with a holy feeling. It's careful.
Nobody offers a burnt roti on purpose.

how: Many Hindu households offer the first portion of cooked food at the home shrine, or to a cow or birds, before the family eats, and the shrine portion is received back as prasad; the Ramakrishna Mission and many seva groups describe service to people as worship.

o: worshiping God through the work that is yours
giving up your job to serve in a temple
the karma your past deeds have earned you

games.q: work as worship — tap the pairs.
p: offered food, received back as a blessing

s: at the end of the Gita, Arjuna still refuses to fight
he says his confusion is gone and he'll do as Krishna says.
offering the first food before eating is a practice in many Hindu homes
the first roti or spoon of rice often goes to the shrine, a cow or the birds.
in karma yoga, feeling holy matters more than doing the work well
the Gita calls yoga skill in action: offered work is careful work.

games.q: same battlefield, same duty. what changed when Arjuna picked up his bow?
o: he found holier work to do instead.
he took up his own work, now held as worship.
he stopped caring how the battle went.
games.why: nothing outside changed. with your own work, worship, says 18.46. and 2.50 adds: yoga is skill in action.

practice: Picture the first real task waiting for you after this, your hands on the keyboard, the wheel, the dishes or the lesson plan, and notice how you usually meet it: rushed, bored, braced.

Now picture doing that same task with care, as if someone you love were going to receive it. If you pray, dedicate it silently, the way the first roti goes to the shrine; if you don't, just let it be done well, for its own sake.

wordCard.voice: Svakarmana, with one's own work. Krishna's last word on karma yoga: with your own work, worship. Offered work is careful work.

orig.note: Sanskrit, Gita 18.46: 'with one's own work, worshiping that one.' sva (own) + karmanā (by work); abhyarcya, having worshiped.

carryVoice: Your line: with your own work, worship. Arjuna picked up his bow. Two hundred sixty-four days, and counting.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 18.72–73 (is your confusion gone? my confusion is gone; I will do your word)
Bhagavad Gita 18.46 (worshiping with one's own work)
Bhagavad Gita 2.50 (yoga is skill in action)
Ramakrishna Mission (founded 1897), motto 'atmano mokshartham jagad hitaya cha'
